extracted.subtask_description: MPEP guidance for evaluating whether claim additional elements render a judicial exception (law of nature, natural phenomenon, abstract idea) patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. §101. Covers when additional elements meaningfully limit the exception, when they are mere instructions to apply it, insignificant extra-solution activity, and field-of-use/technological-environment considerations, with case examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider additional elements individually and in combination
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating whether additional elements meaningfully limit a judicial exception, examiners must assess the claimed additional elements both individually and as an ordered combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single additional element may be enough to qualify as 'significantly more' if it meaningfully limits the exception, but elements that are not significant on their own may, when combined, amount to significantly more (see Diamond v. Diehr; BASCOM). Examiners should, when appropriate, explain on the record why the additional elements meaningfully limit the judicial exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere instructions to apply an exception ('apply it')
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the additional elements are nothing more than a recitation of the judicial exception plus words that instruct to 'apply it' (or equivalents such as implementation on a generic computer). Such recitations do not render the claim eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court cases (Alice, Mayo, Benson) show that simply adding words to apply an abstract idea or law of nature—especially by reciting a generic computer—does not provide an inventive concept. Examiners should explain why alleged additional elements do not meaningfully limit the exception and should consider overlaps with other Step 2B considerations (particular machine/transformation, well-understood/routine/conventional activity). Note that requiring more than 'mere instructions' does not mean claims must be narrow; some broad claims have been held eligible (e.g., McRO, Thales Visionix), and some narrow claims ineligible (e.g., Ultramercial, Electric Power Group).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciting only the idea or outcome (result-oriented claiming)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite only the idea of a solution or the desired outcome—failing to recite details of how the solution is accomplished—are equivalent to saying 'apply it' and do not supply significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claim limitations attempt to cover any solution to an identified problem without restricting how the result is achieved or describing mechanisms, they likely do not add significantly more (see Electric Power Group; Intellectual Ventures v. Symantec). By contrast, claiming a particular solution or a particular way to achieve an outcome can provide significantly more. Example: claims that describe modifying an XML document but provide no specific steps were held ineligible (Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invoking computers or machinery merely as tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a computer or other machinery in its ordinary capacity as a tool to perform an existing process (receive, store, transmit data, etc.) generally does not provide significantly more than the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that simply add a general-purpose computer or common machinery after the fact, or rely on increased speed or efficiency solely from generic computer capabilities, fail to provide an inventive concept (see Alice; TLI Communications; Affinity Labs; Intellectual Ventures I LLC v. Capital One Bank). In contrast, claims that improve computer capabilities or provide improvements to another technology or technical field (e.g., McRO, Enfish) may provide significantly more. Examiners should evaluate whether the computer/machinery is used merely in its ordinary capacity or is integral to a technological improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity versus generality of application
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the claim confines the judicial exception to a particular, practical application (which may provide significantly more) versus claiming broad applicability across many fields (which likely does not).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad claims that generically recite an effect or claim every mode of accomplishing that effect are likely equivalent to adding 'apply it' (see Internet Patents Corp. v. Active Network; O’Reilly v. Morse). Limitations that confine the exception to a particular practical application and are integrated into the claim's steps (e.g., Diehr; BASCOM's filtering tool at a specific location with customizable features) have been found meaningful. A common sign of a non-meaningful limitation is an absence of integration into the claim as a whole (token or incidental additions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant extra-solution activity (pre- and post-solution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether additional elements amount to insignificant 'extra-solution' activity—incidental pre-solution or post-solution steps that are nominal or tangential to the claimed invention and do not add an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extra-solution activity includes things like data gathering before the claimed process or outputting results after it (e.g., printing). The Supreme Court (Flook, Mayo) and subsequent cases treat such insignificant activities, particularly when well-understood or conventional, as not transforming an unpatentable principle into a patentable process. Examiners should evaluate other Step 2B considerations (particular machine/transformation, well-understood/routine/conventional, field-of-use) when determining insignificance. If an extra-solution activity is not integrated or is merely nominal, explain on the record why it does not meaningfully limit the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors for analyzing extra-solution activity
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating whether an additional element is insignificant extra-solution activity, consider whether the limitation is well-known, significant, or merely necessary data gathering/output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1) Well-known: If the extra-solution element is well known (e.g., standard analysis techniques, common XML tags), it may be token extra-solution activity (Bilski; Flook; Intellectual Ventures v. Erie Indem.). 2) Significance: Does the limitation impose meaningful limits on the claim (if not, it may be insignificant; see Ultramercial; Apple v. Ameranth). 3) Necessary data gathering/output: If all uses of the recited judicial exception require the data gathering or outputting, that activity is likely insignificant (Mayo; OIP Technologies). Use these factors plus case examples to justify an eligibility rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of activities treated as insignificant extra-solution activity
rubrics_metrics.description: The guidance enumerates categories and specific examples courts have found to be insignificant extra-solution activity (mere data gathering, selecting data sources, and insignificant applications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere data gathering examples: clinical tests to obtain inputs (In re Grams), testing system responses (In re Meyers), presenting offers and gathering customer-response statistics (OIP Technologies), obtaining transaction info to verify credit cards (CyberSource), updating logs (Ultramercial), measuring biomarker levels (Mayo). Selecting particular data sources: limiting an index to XML tags (Intellectual Ventures v. Erie Indem.), taking only table-based food orders (Ameranth), selecting power-grid info (Electric Power Group). Insignificant application examples: cutting hair after selecting a style (In re Brown), printing/downloading generated menus (Ameranth). Examiners should reference such examples when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field of use / technological environment limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that merely link the judicial exception to a particular field of use or technological environment (e.g., 'apply this formula in petrochemical processes' or 'on a cellular telephone') typically do not amount to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parker v. Flook illustrates that limiting an abstract idea to a particular field is a classic token limitation; more recent cases (Affinity Labs) show that limiting an abstract idea to a device class or environment (e.g., cell phones) often fails to add an inventive concept. A key question is whether the limitation is integrated into the claim to change how the steps are performed (Diehr) versus an incidental or token field-of-use statement. Examples include limiting drug administration to a patient class (Mayo), limiting hedging to commodity providers/consumers (Bilski), or specifying that a process runs on the Internet (FairWarning; Ultramercial).
